The power went out just as Aparna and her father, Akash, started the argument again, so they sat in the dark with one candle between them.
"Last Sunday you said I could go to the late show if I finished my project," Aparna said. "Your exact words."
"I said we'd discuss it once the project was done," Akash said. "I would never promise a late show."
Both were certain. Aparna remembered his smile, because she had been so happy that day. Akash remembered feeling uneasy, because he had worried all week about the last bus home.
In the candlelight, Aparna's younger brother spoke up. "I was there. Nobody said 'late show'. You both said 'maybe'."
They looked at each other. Neither spoke for a moment. Then Akash said, "Let's decide it now, and write it down."

qa.q: What did Aparna say her father had promised last Sunday?
qa.a: She said he had promised she could go to the late show if she finished her project.

qa.q: Why does Aparna remember a clear promise?
qa.a: She was so happy that day that she remembered his smile, and her hopes seem to have turned a "maybe" into a yes in her memory.

qa.q: What choice at the end could prevent the next argument like this?
qa.a: Akash suggests deciding now and writing it down, so the plan no longer depends on two memories coloured by feelings.

qa.q: How might the younger brother feel stepping into the argument?
qa.a: He might feel nervous about contradicting both of them, but also that someone had to say what he heard, since each was so sure.

grounding: It shows a teenager and a parent who each remember an argument differently, shaped by hope on one side and worry on the other.

"You called me useless," Vishal said, dropping his bag by the shoe rack. "On Tuesday. About the maths marks."
Usha, his mother, put down the vegetable knife. "I said the marks were useless for the effort you'd put in. I didn't call you anything."
The argument had happened in the kitchen of their flat in a crowded Chennai colony, with the pressure cooker whistling. Vishal had lain awake that night going over it, and each time the word sounded harsher. Usha had spent the week thinking about how gently she had tried to speak, and her memory had grown gentler too.
Neither of them was lying, and neither could prove a thing.
"Maybe the cooker was loud," Usha said at last. "What I meant was that I know you can do better. I'm sorry it came out like that."
Vishal nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where did the argument about the maths marks happen?
qa.a: It happened in the kitchen of their flat, with the pressure cooker whistling.

qa.q: Why does Vishal remember being called useless?
qa.a: He went over the argument again and again that night, and each time the word sounded harsher, so hurt feelings reshaped the memory.

qa.q: What choice by Usha eased things?
qa.a: Instead of proving her version, Usha allowed that the cooker was loud, explained what she meant and said sorry for how it came out.

qa.q: How has Usha's week of thinking shaped her own memory of Tuesday?
qa.a: She kept thinking about how gently she had tried to speak, so her memory grew gentler too, which made Vishal's version sound unfair to her.

grounding: It shows a teenage son and his mother remembering the same argument differently, each version shaped by later feelings and thoughts.

Last spring, Kamal and I nearly fell out over a client call. I was certain the client had agreed to a Friday deadline. Kamal was just as certain they had said Monday.
The old me would have said, "You weren't listening." Instead I said, "I remember Friday, but let me check." We had both taken notes. Mine said "Fri?" with a question mark. Kamal's said "Mon, confirm by mail." The email, when we found it, said Monday.
What surprised me was how sure I had felt. That feeling had misled me, not Kamal.
Now I start with, "This is how I remember it," and after big calls I send a short summary email the same day. Kamal teases me that I'm the team's recorder. I'm Arohi, and I'm fine with that.

qa.q: What did Arohi's note from the call say?
qa.a: Arohi's note said "Fri?" with a question mark.

qa.q: What did Arohi realise about feeling sure, once the email was found?
qa.a: Arohi realised the strong feeling of certainty had been wrong, not Kamal, and that feeling sure is not the same as being right.

qa.a: Arohi now starts with "This is how I remember it" and sends a short summary email the same day after big calls.

Counsellor's note, Thursday
Parth, 8, came to see me after his aunt, Rajni, had asked him about a scratch on his cousin's bicycle. She had asked, "You scratched it while riding, didn't you? You rode it into the gate?" By evening Parth was saying he had ridden it into the gate. He told me the same, looking at the floor.

I'm Kiran, Salma's roommate, so I heard this one live. Salma was video-calling her family and said, "Remember when Abbu carried me on his shoulders through the flood water? I was holding the umbrella." She described it all: the brown water, the red umbrella, the shop shutters.
Her mother went quiet. Then her brother said, "Salma, there was never a flood. You saw that in a film at Khala's house."
Salma laughed at first, then didn't. After the call she sat on her bed for a long time with her knees pulled up. She said, "I can still feel the umbrella handle."
I don't know what was going on in her head. I just made tea and didn't take either side.

When a delivery scooter skidded into the gate of the Bengaluru apartment complex, Reena, the society's young secretary, reached the lobby within minutes. Joseph, the watchman, was shaking. A resident said, "The rider was speeding, madam. Surely he was speeding?"
Reena raised a hand. "Let's not guess. Joseph, tell me what you saw, from the start." Joseph described the rain, the rider braking and the wheel sliding.
She typed it on her phone right there, with the time, and asked two other residents the same open question separately.
Joseph kept saying, "It was so frightening." Reena said, "I believe you. It must have been." In her notes she marked the speed as "unclear", since the three accounts differed.
Later, the rider's family thanked her for a fair account.

qa.q: What did Joseph describe from the start?
qa.a: Joseph described the rain, the rider braking and the wheel sliding.

qa.q: Why did Reena stop the resident's question about speeding?
qa.a: She seems to know that "Surely he was speeding?" can plant an answer, and she wanted Joseph's own account first.

qa.q: Which choices made Reena's account fair?
qa.a: She asked open questions, typed notes at once with the time, spoke to people separately and marked the speed "unclear" when accounts differed.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt when Reena said, "I believe you. It must have been"?
qa.a: Joseph probably felt taken seriously and calmer, since the fear was accepted even while the details were checked.

grounding: It shows a young secretary who avoids leading questions, records accounts at once and respects a witness's fear without treating it as proof.

In my first month at the local paper, a small fire broke out in the fish market. I rushed there and asked a stall owner, "It started from the gas cylinder, didn't it?" She nodded, and I nearly printed it.
Thomas, my editor, read my notes and asked, "Who said 'cylinder' first, you or her?" I went quiet. It was me.
Now I do it differently. I ask, "What did you see?" and let people talk. I write my notes within the hour, with times, and I mark what I saw, what I was told and what I guessed. When someone cries describing the smoke, I take that seriously; the fear is real. But I don't print their guess about the cause as fact.
I'm Noor, and I learnt that the hard way, in front of a fish stall.

qa.q: What did Noor first ask the stall owner?
qa.a: Noor asked, "It started from the gas cylinder, didn't it?"

qa.q: Why did Noor go quiet when Thomas asked who said "cylinder" first?
qa.a: Noor realised the idea had come from the question, not the stall owner, and felt embarrassed at nearly printing a planted answer.

qa.q: What habits did Noor build after that turning point?
qa.a: Noor asks "What did you see?", writes notes within the hour with times, and marks what was seen, told and guessed.

qa.q: How might the stall owner be affected if the planted cause had been printed?
qa.a: The stall owner would be quoted saying something never actually seen, and people might blame the wrong thing for the fire.

grounding: It shows a young reporter who learns to avoid leading questions, record facts soon after, and respect witnesses' fear without printing guesses as proof.

Teacher's note, Class 3, Wednesday
Madhav told his group today that a snake came into our classroom last week and hid in the cupboard, and that I caught it with a broom. He was very upset when the others said it wasn't true, and he went red defending it.
No snake came. I asked him gently, "Where do you think you saw it?" He paused and said there is a cartoon where a teacher catches a snake with a broom. Then, slowly: "Maybe that was the cartoon."
He wasn't lying; he believed it. I told the group so. Tomorrow we'll play a short game called "Seen, heard or watched?", where children sort things they remember.
Shankar

qa.a: He said it hid in the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Madhav go red defending the snake story?
qa.a: He believed it fully and felt hurt when others doubted him, because the cartoon memory felt like something from his own classroom.

qa.q: What game did Shankar plan, and how could it help?
qa.a: "Seen, heard or watched?", where children sort their memories, which trains them to notice where each memory came from.

qa.q: How might the group feel after Shankar says Madhav wasn't lying?
qa.a: They might stop teasing him and understand that mixing up a cartoon with real life can happen to anyone.

grounding: It shows a boy who sincerely defends a classroom memory that came from a cartoon, with the source lost.
